logline: Five young offenders on community service survive a freak electrical storm that grants each of them a superpower - and immediately find themselves in far more trouble than any ASBO ever caused.

renewal.note: Misfits ran for five series on E4 from November 2009 to December 2013, concluding after the majority of the original cast had departed. The show ended on its own terms without a formal cancellation announcement.

bollymeter.basis: A 100% Rotten Tomatoes score on debut and a 2010 BAFTA for Best Drama Series reflect a consensus that the show's irreverent British street energy and Robert Sheehan's breakout performance redefined the superhero genre on television.

pull_quotes.text: A thoroughly enjoyable concept, very well done, in the safe hands of a capable cast.

seasons.review_body: Series 1 premiered on E4 in November 2009 and immediately won the 2010 BAFTA Television Award for Best Drama Series - a striking achievement for a low-budget youth comedy about community service workers in a southeast London estate. Critics gave it a 100% Rotten Tomatoes debut score. The consensus fixed on writer Howard Overman's gift for embedding genuine darkness inside crude comedy, and on Robert Sheehan's Nathan as one of the decade's great British TV characters: disarmingly witty, self-destructive, and impossible to dismiss. The show drew comparison to Skins and Dead Set but quickly established its own register: the superhero genre rebuilt from scratch by writers who found it absurd. The audience scored it 8.1 on IMDb across all five series.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 1
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The pilot drops five immediately distinguishable archetypes - the charmer, the thug, the quiet girl, the athlete, the outsider - into community service and then into a storm that changes all the rules. What separates it from a dozen similar high-concept British dramas is the tone: gleefully inappropriate, genuinely funny, and darker than any network equivalent would permit.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The storm sequence itself - the moment the genre premise snaps into place and the show declares what kind of beast it is.

critic_note.text: A thoroughly enjoyable concept, very well done, in the safe hands of a capable cast.

bollymeter.basis: An 86% Rotten Tomatoes score reflects strong second-series approval while acknowledging the slight decline from the debut's perfect rating; the season deepens the mythology without fully matching the first-series freshness.

seasons.review_body: Series 2 aired in November and December 2010, adding a seventh episode and deepening the mythology around what the storm's powers actually mean. Critics scored it at 86% on Rotten Tomatoes, acknowledging the show's consistent irreverence and Robert Sheehan's continued dominance while noting the diminishing surprise factor of a concept now familiar to its audience. The season introduced a villain arc and experimented with power-swapping as a narrative device, which generated some of the series' most formally inventive episodes. Sheehan remained the critical and commercial anchor; his departure after this series would pose the central challenge for subsequent runs.
seasons.season_over_season: Expands the mythology and episode count but trades first-series shock value for more sustained character arcs; the 86% score marks a small but real step back from the debut.

bollymeter.basis: A 100% Rotten Tomatoes score on a small sample reflects critics' generous reading of the transition series; the show rebuilt around Joe Gilgun's Rudy competently but the audience registered Sheehan's absence in viewing figures.

seasons.review_body: Series 3, airing from October 2011, was the transition season: Robert Sheehan had left, and the show needed a new anchor. Joe Gilgun's Rudy - foul-mouthed, self-contradicting, occasionally tender - proved a credible replacement. Critics on Rotten Tomatoes scored the series at 100% on a limited sample, and the general critical read was that Misfits had weathered its biggest cast challenge more gracefully than expected. The eight-episode run introduced the power-selling concept that would drive the show's later seasons and demonstrated that the format was genuinely flexible. Audiences remained loyal, with the IMDb aggregate holding steady across all five series.
seasons.season_over_season: Navigates the loss of its most recognisable performer via Gilgun's credible replacement; critics were more generous than the narrative transition perhaps warranted.

bollymeter.basis: A 78% Rotten Tomatoes score and critic consensus noting lost momentum after further cast changes track a show seeking its identity with a third roster; still watchable, no longer essential.

seasons.review_body: Series 4 aired October to December 2012 and sustained further cast changes as the show cycled toward its third roster of main characters. Critics scored it at 78% on Rotten Tomatoes, with the consensus noting that while the crude humour and E4 production formula remained intact, the ongoing loss of original cast members had diluted the group chemistry the first two series built their reputation on. The show retained its dark register and Gilgun remained a reliable presence, but the sense of discovery that had defined the debut years was no longer available to it.
seasons.season_over_season: Further cast turnover drags the RT score to 78%; the show retains its voice but loses the ensemble chemistry that made earlier series distinctive.

bollymeter.basis: A 100% Rotten Tomatoes score on a very small critical sample and a strong final-season narrative focus suggest the show closed on an upswing relative to Series 4, though the audience for it had contracted substantially.

seasons.review_body: The fifth and final series ran from October to December 2013, bringing the show to a close with a finale that attempted to honour the spirit of the original premise. Critics on Rotten Tomatoes scored it at 100% on a limited sample. The general read was that the show achieved a more purposeful conclusion than its mid-run drift suggested it would manage. For those who had tracked all five series, the finale delivered a respectable end; for viewers seeking the anarchic energy of Series 1, the distance was too great. The show ended without fanfare, its BAFTA-winning first series still the definitive argument for its place in British television history.
seasons.season_over_season: Closes with more purpose than Series 4 suggested possible; the small critical sample inflates the RT score, but the finale is a genuine attempt at a proper ending.
